title: Distributions On Spheres
notes: Open by moving the class from a circular sample space to the unit sphere. The essential change is not merely one more coordinate; it is the loss of a preferred chart and the arrival of axial observations, where a measured line identifies opposite unit vectors.

title: Lecture Route
notes: Use the route as the contract for the lecture. We first decide what the observation is, then choose summaries that survive rotation, then place model families on top of those summaries, and finally read the two asymptotic stories without mixing them.

title: Sphere Versus Axis
notes: Emphasize that a point on the sphere and an unoriented axis live in different statistical spaces. The same recorded vector can be meaningful as a signed direction or only as a line through the origin, and the summary must respect that scientific choice.

title: Resultant Or Inertia
notes: The mean resultant is excellent when the cloud has one oriented pole, but it deliberately cancels an antipodal cloud. The inertia matrix keeps quadratic information, so the equality between x x transpose and minus x minus x transpose becomes the bridge to axial statistics.

title: Invariant Scaffold
notes: This is the algebraic safety rail for the chapter. Trace one, positive semidefiniteness, the variance decomposition, and rotation-equivariance are not optional decorations; they are quick tests that the computation still belongs to a spherical sample space.

title: Readable Spherical Diagnostics
notes: A Lambert disk is useful because it lets a projected page distinguish near and far hemispheres while keeping area distortion controlled. Pair it with an inertia spectrum so the eye sees both a point cloud and the coordinate-free quadratic summary.

title: Fisher And von Mises-Fisher
notes: Present the Fisher model as the spherical analogue of a one-pole concentration model. The sufficient statistic is the projection onto the mean direction, so increasing kappa steepens density along one axis without making the antipodal point equally likely.

title: Normalization Through Projection
notes: For S two, reduce the normalization check to the scalar t equal mu dot x. The uniform sphere contributes a flat density in t on minus one to one, so the exponential tilt can be integrated directly and checked numerically.

title: Axial Families
notes: Watson and Bingham models answer the question that Fisher does not: what if signs are irrelevant or the spread is better described by a quadratic form? Ask students to inspect whether mass lives at two poles, around an equator, or in an oval axial lobe.

title: Decision Evidence
notes: The numbers make the modeling choice concrete. The directional synthetic sample has a large resultant and a dominant inertia eigenvalue; the antipodal sample has nearly zero resultant but still has a dominant eigenvector, so the appropriate summary changes.

title: Distribution Theory Objects
notes: Before tests and confidence cones, the class needs the random objects whose distributions will be approximated. Resultant length, projected coordinates, and inertia eigenstructure each answer a different geometric question, and each has a different null behavior.

title: High-Concentration Limit
notes: Keep the limit local. When kappa is large, observations near the pole can be represented in a tangent plane, and the scaled tangent coordinates look Gaussian. The radial statistic two kappa times one minus the projection behaves like a chi-square variable.

title: High-Dimensional Uniform Limit
notes: Separate high dimension from high concentration. A uniform point on a large sphere is not near a chosen pole, but any fixed coordinate is small with Gaussian scaling. The square root p factor is the natural magnifying glass for that coordinate.

title: Applied Modeling Checklist
notes: Turn the theory into a workflow. First decide whether signs matter, then verify unit norms, then inspect resultant and inertia evidence, then choose a one-pole, axial, girdle, or quadratic model family before moving to inference.

title: Chapter Takeaways
notes: Close by tying the chapter to later inference on spheres. A reliable spherical analysis starts with the sample space, uses invariant summaries, chooses a model whose symmetry matches the data, and treats tangent or high-dimensional approximations as checks rather than slogans.
